1814: Fuerza Dread at Santos Rock 2025: Commitment, emotion, and roots reggae

At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal, Fuerza Dread’s appearance was one of the event’s most moving moments. The band from Puntarenas, with nearly two decades of experience, performed its signature roots reggae blended with funk, jazz, and rock.

t the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal, Fuerza Dread’s appearance was one of the event’s most moving moments. The band from Puntarenas, with nearly two decades of experience, performed its signature roots reggae blended with funk, jazz, and rock.

We had the opportunity to speak with the members at Cafetería Coopedota, one of the event’s official sponsors, where they shared their impressions of the festival and the emotional bond they formed with the audience.
“Without a doubt, the people… hearing everyone sing the songs… it actually gave me goosebumps.”

The band described the experience as a moment that reaffirmed their commitment to music and to the project they have been building for years. “It makes us feel very committed to the project and the work we are doing,” they said.

They also shared their joy at the festival’s diverse lineup, where ska, metal, reggae, and rock came together in a single day. “There was a little bit of everything,” they said, appreciating the range of musical approaches that enrich the national scene.
Another highlight was the opportunity to play outside the Central Valley and the pleasant surprise it brought:
“Sometimes you have this idea that the whole scene happens in the Central Valley… but arriving and receiving that warmth here in Dota… it was incredible.”
Finally, they shared a message for those starting out in music: “Fear will always be part of any process… but if we turn that fear into an ‘I can,’ that is where everything begins.”

Fuerza Dread delivered a memorable show at Santos Rock 2025 and reaffirmed that its place in Costa Rican music is built on authenticity, consistent work, and the positive message it conveys through every note.

2137: Artists from Los Santos represent Costa Rica on an international album for Palestine

Three Costa Rican artists from the Los Santos region—Jenny Abarca, rapper Dopa G, and Chejo G—are taking part in the international album “Palestina Libre,” a musical project against genocide and in defense of human rights, bringing together 50 artists from 13 countries in a collaborative collection of 40 songs for freedom and peace.

hree Costa Rican artists from the Los Santos region—Jenny Abarca, rapper Dopa G, and Chejo G—are taking part in the international album “Palestina Libre,” a musical project against genocide and in defense of human rights, bringing together 50 artists from 13 countries in a collaborative collection of 40 songs for freedom and peace.
The album, officially released on August 15, 2025 on all digital platforms, is an expression of art and activism in which music becomes a tool for speaking out, resistance, and hope

Jenny Abarca on the Santos Rock stage

Costa Rica brings its own voice
Costa Rica’s contribution to the album is a song written by Jenny Abarca together with Chejo G and Dopa G, carrying a powerful message from the mountains of Los Santos to listeners around the world.
“We joined this project from the heart, convinced that art can break down borders, denounce injustice, and build bridges of solidarity,” said Jenny Abarca.
The three artists bring an authentic perspective rooted in their regional identity, adding their talent to a cause that demands international justice and peace for the Palestinian people.

Palestina Libre began as an initiative by Spanish musicians José Riaza and Eloy Acosta, who mobilized the international artistic community to create a collective album in response to the cruelty of genocide. The production has the support of the NGO Más Música, Menos Balas and the record label SocSub (Sociedad Subterránea).
Alongside the album, launch concerts, audiovisual showcases, and art exhibitions will take place in different countries, with active participation from the musicians involved.
2561: When the classroom becomes a stage: Zavaleta Music Fest 2025
On November 3, Colegio Técnico Profesional José Daniel Flores Zavaleta in Santa María de Dota enjoyed a day filled with music and community at the first Zavaleta Music Fest.

On November 3, Colegio Técnico Profesional José Daniel Flores Zavaleta in Santa María de Dota enjoyed a day filled with music and community at the first Zavaleta Music Fest. It was more than a concert: it was the culmination of an educational project in which art became a bridge between the classroom and the stage.
The idea did not begin as a formal festival:

“We thought of it as a classroom activity more than a festival. It is a project for tenth and eleventh graders. We did not just say: let’s put on a festival,” explained music teacher Heyner Rivera, the driving force behind the event.

What began as a classroom activity, with rehearsals and songs, grew as students made the project their own. Little by little, music became more than a subject: it became a source of creativity and collaboration. An academic activity turned into a community experience where everyone found a role, whether onstage or in logistics, decoration, or sound.

The students’ own enthusiasm transformed the idea into something much bigger. When they noticed that their work had an impact, that their classmates were joining in, and that the art they created moved other people, they stopped seeing it as an assignment and began experiencing it as a shared commitment.
The festival provided a platform for the school’s art and for the organizing talents of people who do not usually get involved in music.

“They gradually got involved, and when they saw how many people were signing up to help, they felt motivated and started bringing whatever was needed: decorations, this and that,” teacher Rivera recalls enthusiastically.

Performances ranged from Spanish-language rock classics such as Soda Stereo to more contemporary artists such as Mon Laferte and Carla Morrison. There was also room for guest artists and original compositions. The program had two blocks, with an intermission featuring food prepared by the school community.
For teacher Rivera, Zavaleta Music Fest is also an investment in local artistic identity:

“What I am exploring with the students is rock. I go in that direction because it is the root. After the root, you can move into other rhythms,” he explained, noting that rock represents the local musical output of the Los Santos region.
As part of their learning process, students researched the region’s music scene, from pioneering bands such as Anestesia Local to current names such as Santo Remedio and Rana Bruja.
“Ending with a concert is the practical side of all that knowledge,” the teacher said.

Advertising design students accompanied every performance through the lens of Zavaleta Studio, the school’s photography and video studio. Its team documented the entire event and captured the festival’s best moments. Thanks to their work, we can now relive the energy of the day.

At Santos Rock, we warmly celebrate initiatives like this. Alongside talent, there is identity, collective work, and passion for what is ours. This new generation is arriving with strength and love for its music. We firmly believe they will take to the stages of the future and continue building our culture.
